items.prose: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has no real eigenvalues: they are $\pm 1.414i$.
items.question: What is its largest singular value $\sigma_1$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ and take square roots of its eigenvalues.

byKey.noroot: 4 is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$. Take its square root.
byKey.eig: 1.414 is the size of the complex eigenvalues. Singular values come from $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.

explain.text: The columns of $\mathbf{A}$ are $(0, -1)$ and $(2, 0)$, so $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \operatorname{diag}(1, 4)$. Then $\sigma = 2, 1$. A matrix with no real eigenvalues still has an SVD.

options.why: $\mathbf{A}$ acts on input directions $\mathbf{v}_i$. Going back from $\mathbf{u}_1$ needs $\mathbf{A}^T$.
That would make $\mathbf{v}_1$ an eigenvector. In general $\mathbf{A}$ turns $\mathbf{v}_1$ into a different direction, $\mathbf{u}_1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Transpose the SVD and read it right to left.

explain.text: Transposing gives $\mathbf{A}^T = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{U}^T$. It turns $\mathbf{u}_1$ onto the first axis, stretches by $\sigma_1$, and turns that onto $\mathbf{v}_1$.

items.prose: A matrix has singular values 6, 3 and 2.
items.question: What share of the energy does its best rank-1 approximation keep?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $\sigma_1^2$ by the sum of all $\sigma_i^2$.

byKey.nosq: You divided $6$ by $11$. Energy uses squares: $36/49$.

explain.text: The energy is $36 + 9 + 4 = 49$, and $\mathbf{A}_1$ keeps $\sigma_1^2 = 36$ of it.

items.prose: The same matrix, with singular values 6, 3 and 2.
items.question: What is the error energy of its best rank-2 approximation?

feedback.correct: Only $\sigma_3 = 2$ is dropped, so the error energy is 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the singular values that rank 2 drops and add them.

byKey.nosq: 2 is $\sigma_3$ itself. Energy is its square.
byKey.two: 13 drops two pieces. Rank 2 keeps two and drops one.

explain.text: By Eckart–Young the best rank-2 error is $\sigma_3^2 = 4$, which is $4/49 = 8.2\%$ of the energy. No other rank-2 matrix gets closer.

items.question: What share of the variance does PC1 explain?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both eigenvalues, then divide the larger by their sum.

byKey.half: Equal variances do not mean an equal split. The correlation makes the common move bigger: $\lambda_1 = 4$.
byKey.sq: You squared the eigenvalues. They are variances already.

explain.text: PC1 is $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ with variance $3 + 1 = 4$; PC2 is $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$ with variance 2. The total is the trace, 6.

items.prose: An analyst runs PCA on daily returns of two stocks that both rallied hard all month. She forms $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}/(n-1)$ from the raw returns.
items.question: What does her first component mostly capture?

options.text: The direction from the origin to the average day
How the two stocks move together day to day
options.why: That is what PC1 captures after demeaning. Without it, the large mean adds $\tfrac{n}{n-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^T$, which dominates.

options.text: Nothing changes: the mean cancels in the covariance
options.why: The mean only cancels if you subtract it. Raw $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ keeps it.

feedback.correct: Without demeaning, PC1 chases the mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what raw $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ contains beyond the covariance.

explain.text: Raw $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}/(n-1) = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} + \tfrac{n}{n-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^T$. A large mean makes the second term dominate, so PC1 points along $\boldsymbol{\mu}$. Subtract column means first.

items.prose: A demeaned data matrix $\mathbf{X}$ has 17 rows and two columns. Its singular values are 12 and 4.
items.question: What share of the variance does PC1 explain?

byKey.nosq: You compared $12/16$. Square the singular values first: $144/160$.

explain.text: $\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2/(n-1)$ gives 9 and 1. The factor $n - 1$ cancels in the share, which is $144/160 = 90\%$.

items.question: What is its smaller singular value $\sigma_2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Form the $2 \times 2$ matrix $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ and take square roots of its eigenvalues.

byKey.noroot: 2 is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ (and also $\sigma_1$). Take the square root of the smaller eigenvalue, 2.
byKey.zero: The columns are independent, so neither singular value is 0. The zero eigenvalue belongs to the $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T$.

explain.text: Column dot products give $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalues $3 \pm 1$. So $\sigma_1 = 2$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt2 \approx 1.414$.
